questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the angles formed measures 65°. What is the measure of the corresponding angle?
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Therefore, the corresponding angle also measures 65°.
questions.trap: Students confuse corresponding angles (equal) with co-interior angles (supplementary). The co-interior angle would be 180° − 65° = 115°, which is option C.

questions.question: Lines l and m are parallel and are cut by a transversal t. An interior angle of 110° is formed at line l, on the left side of t. What is the measure of the alternate interior angle at line m?
questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal when two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. The alternate interior angle is between the two parallel lines, on the opposite side of the transversal — it equals 110°.
questions.trap: Students think alternate interior angles are supplementary (giving 70°). They are equal, not supplementary. Co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary.
questions.ets_note: Stated angle is exterior, so 'alternate interior angle' is ill-defined; no figure.

changes: made the given angle an interior angle so 'alternate interior' is defined

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A co-interior (same-side interior) angle measures 72°. What is the measure, in degrees, of the other co-interior angle?
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles (also called same-side interior or consecutive interior angles) are supplementary — they sum to 180°. So the other angle = 180° − 72° = 108°.
questions.trap: Students write 72° thinking co-interior angles are equal like alternate interior angles. They are supplementary, not equal.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 315 235" width="315" height="235" role="img"><line x1="30.0" y1="75.0" x2="285.0" y2="75.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="30.0" y1="155.0" x2="285.0" y2="155.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 142 71 l 10 4 l -10 4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 142 151 l 10 4 l -10 4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="130.4" y1="33.0" x2="183.6" y2="197.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 160.0 75.0 A 16 16 0 0 1 148.9 90.2" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="190.0" y="95.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">72°</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: "Co-interior" is not ETS terminology; one-step recall.

questions.question: A transversal crosses two parallel lines, forming an exterior angle of 55° at the first line. What is the measure of the alternate exterior angle at the second line?
questions.explanation: Alternate exterior angles are equal when lines are parallel. The alternate exterior angle also measures 55°.
questions.trap: Students add instead of recognizing equality, or confuse alternate exterior (equal) with co-interior (supplementary).
questions.ets_note: Which angle is 55 is unspecified; no figure; textbook terminology.

changes: stated the given angle is an exterior angle

questions.question: Lines p and q are parallel. A transversal crosses both, creating an interior angle of 130° at line p. What is the measure of the interior angle at line q on the same side of the transversal?
questions.explanation: Co-interior (same-side interior) angles are supplementary. The co-interior angle = 180° − 130° = 50°.
questions.trap: Students choose 130° thinking co-interior angles are equal (they're not — those are alternate interior angles).
questions.ets_note: No figure; "co-interior" non-ETS and x position ambiguous. Options 60 and 310 are filler.

changes: 'angle x' placed (interior) and 'co-interior' replaced with 'interior angle ... on the same side'

questions.question:
Lines a and b are parallel and are cut by a transversal. One interior angle measures 80°.

Quantity A: The measure of the angle that is alternate interior to the 80° angle
Quantity B: 80°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal when lines are parallel. So the alternate interior angle = 80° = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students think alternate interior angles are supplementary (making Quantity A = 100°) and choose A.
questions.ets_note: Quantity A convoluted and ambiguous; QC with no figure; trivial.

changes: made the 80° angle the reference for the alternate interior angle

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. The transversal makes an angle of 40° with the first parallel line (measured as an acute angle). What is the measure, in degrees, of the obtuse angle the transversal makes with the same line at that intersection?
questions.explanation: The two angles at any intersection on a straight line are supplementary. So the obtuse angle = 180° − 40° = 140°.
questions.trap: Students apply the parallel-line angle rules across intersections when the question asks about both angles at a single intersection.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 315 235" width="315" height="235" role="img"><line x1="30.0" y1="75.0" x2="285.0" y2="75.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="30.0" y1="155.0" x2="285.0" y2="155.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 142 71 l 10 4 l -10 4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 142 151 l 10 4 l -10 4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="59.3" y1="33.0" x2="254.7" y2="197.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 125.3 75.0 A 16 16 0 0 1 121.6 85.3" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="155.3" y="95.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">40°</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Clumsy phrasing '(measured as an acute angle)'; trivial.

questions.question: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. At the first intersection, four angles are formed. One angle measures 75°. How many of the remaining three angles at that same intersection also measure 75°?
questions.explanation: At any intersection, opposite (vertical) angles are equal. So there are 2 angles of 75° and 2 angles of 105° at that intersection. Among the remaining 3 angles (besides the given one), exactly 1 also measures 75° — its vertical angle.
questions.trap: Students say 2, counting the given angle itself as one of the 75° angles, and then state there are 2 total. The question asks how many of the OTHER three measure 75°, which is exactly 1.
questions.ets_note: Easy, plain; option 4 impossible filler.

questions.question: Lines m and n are parallel. A transversal makes a 90° angle with line m. What angle does it make with line n?
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when lines are parallel. Since the transversal is perpendicular to m (90°), it is also perpendicular to n (90°). A line perpendicular to one of two parallel lines is perpendicular to both.
questions.trap: Students think the angle changes at the second parallel line. It does not — corresponding angles are equal.
questions.ets_note: Trivial recall.

questions.question:
Two parallel lines are intersected by a transversal that is perpendicular to both lines.

Quantity A: The sum of two interior angles on the same side of the transversal
Quantity B: The sum of two alternate interior angles
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: When the transversal is perpendicular, each interior angle = 90°. Co-interior sum = 90° + 90° = 180°. Alternate interior angles are equal (each = 90°), so their sum = 90° + 90° = 180°. Quantity A = Quantity B = 180°.
questions.trap: Students assume co-interior angles always produce a greater sum. When the transversal is perpendicular, both sums equal 180°.
questions.ets_note: 'Co-interior' is non-ETS terminology; degenerate perpendicular case trivialises item.

changes: "co-interior" -> "interior angles on the same side of the transversal"
"makes an angle of 90 degrees with" -> "is perpendicular to"

questions.question: A transversal cuts two parallel lines. At the upper intersection, the angle to the left of the transversal above the parallel line is 120°. What is the angle to the right of the transversal below the parallel line at the same (upper) intersection?
questions.explanation: The angle to the right of the transversal below the upper parallel line is the vertical angle to the given 120°. Vertical angles are equal. So the answer is 120°.
questions.trap: Students compute 180° − 120° = 60°, thinking it is a supplementary adjacent angle. Vertical angles are across the intersection, not adjacent.
questions.ets_note: Verbal angle location with no figure is clumsy; ETS would show a diagram.

questions.question: Lines l and m are parallel and are intersected by a transversal. Two corresponding angles have measures (3x)° and (x + 60)°. What is the value of x?
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal: 3x = x + 60. Solving: 2x = 60, so x = 30.
questions.trap: Students set up 3x + (x + 60) = 180° thinking corresponding angles are supplementary. They are equal.
questions.ets_note: 'Find x' is non-ETS; no figure, verbal angle description is clumsy.

changes: "Find x" -> "What is the value of x?"
replaced clumsy verbal position description with plain corresponding-angles statement; same equation 3x = x + 60

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. At the upper parallel line, the interior angle on the right of the transversal measures 115°. What is the measure of the alternate interior angle at the lower parallel line?
questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles lie between the two parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal, and when the lines are parallel they are equal. So the alternate interior angle at the lower line, on the left of the transversal, also measures 115°.
questions.trap: Students subtract from 180° and answer 65°, treating the pair as same-side interior angles, which are supplementary, rather than alternate interior angles, which are equal. 65° is the measure of the interior angle on the right at the lower line.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 315 235" width="315" height="235" role="img"><line x1="30.0" y1="75.0" x2="285.0" y2="75.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="30.0" y1="155.0" x2="285.0" y2="155.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 142 71 l 10 4 l -10 4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 142 151 l 10 4 l -10 4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="195.2" y1="33.0" x2="118.8" y2="197.0" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 191.7 75.0 A 16 16 0 0 1 168.9 89.5" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="221.7" y="95.0" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start" style="">115°</text></svg>
questions.ets_note: Stem says left interior angle is 115 but figure marks the right-side interior angle; left would be 65.

changes: changed 'on the left of the transversal' to 'on the right' in the stem, which is the angle the attached SVG actually marks 115°; on the left the angle is 65°, so the stem and the figure disagreed about which angle was given
named the position of the alternate interior angle in the explanation and corrected the trap's claim about where 65° sits
added a figure description, which the item lacked

questions.figure_description: Two horizontal parallel lines, each marked with an arrowhead, cut by a transversal that runs from upper right to lower left. At the upper line, the interior angle lying to the right of the transversal is marked 115°.

questions.question: Lines l and m are parallel and are cut by a transversal t. One interior angle at line l measures (4x − 10)°, and the interior angle at line m on the same side of t measures (2x + 30)°. What is the value of x, to the nearest tenth?
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles are supplementary: (4x − 10) + (2x + 30) = 180. Simplify: 6x + 20 = 180 → 6x = 160 → x = 160/6 ≈ 26.7.
questions.trap: Students set the angles equal (as if they were alternate interior angles): 4x − 10 = 2x + 30 → 2x = 40 → x = 20.
questions.ets_note: Ambiguous which angles are meant; non-integer answer approximated as 26.7; 'Find x' phrasing.

changes: 'Find x' -> 'What is the value of x'
'co-interior' -> interior angles on the same side of t
added rounding instruction so 26.7 is exact-to-spec

questions.question: Lines p and q are parallel. A transversal creates an angle of (5x + 15)° at line p and an alternate interior angle of (3x + 47)° at line q. What is the measure, in degrees, of each alternate interior angle?
questions.explanation: Alternate interior angles are equal: 5x + 15 = 3x + 47 → 2x = 32 → x = 16. Each angle = 5(16) + 15 = 80 + 15 = 95°. Verify: 3(16) + 47 = 48 + 47 = 95°. ✓
questions.trap: Students add the expressions to 180° (as if they were co-interior): 8x + 62 = 180 → x = 14.75, giving incorrect angle measures.
questions.ets_note: Stem names alternate interior angles, giving the setup; ETS would give a figure.

questions.question:
Lines j and k are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Angle A at line j measures (2y + 10)°. The angle at line k that corresponds to angle A measures (y + 55)°.
Quantity A: y
Quantity B: 45
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal when lines are parallel: 2y + 10 = y + 55 → y = 45. Quantity A = 45 = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students confuse 'corresponding angle' with 'co-interior supplement' and set up (2y + 10) + (y + 55) = 180°, giving 3y + 65 = 180 → y = 38.3, then say Quantity B is greater.
questions.ets_note: 'Co-interior angle' vs 'corresponding angle' conflated; no figure; confusing.

changes: removed 'co-interior', which contradicted 'corresponding' in the same stem

questions.question: Lines l and m are parallel, cut by transversal t. One of the eight angles formed measures 70°. Select all angle measures that must appear among the eight angles formed at the two intersections.
questions.explanation: If one angle is 70°, its supplement is 110°. At each intersection, vertical angles produce: 70°, 70°, 110°, 110°. The full 8 angles across both intersections are all either 70° or 110°. Options C, D, and E need not appear.
questions.trap: Students include C (90°) thinking parallel lines always create right angles — they only do when the transversal is perpendicular.
questions.ets_note: Plain textbook angle fact; D and E are throwaway distractors.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, line DE is drawn parallel to BC, with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = 6, DB = 4, and DE = 9, what is the length of BC?
questions.explanation: By the Triangle Proportionality Theorem, DE/BC = AD/AB. AB = AD + DB = 6 + 4 = 10. So 9/BC = 6/10 → BC = 90/6 = 15.
questions.trap: Students use AD/DB = DE/BC, i.e., 6/4 = 9/BC → BC = 6, using the part-to-part ratio instead of the part-to-whole ratio AD/AB.

questions.question: Three parallel lines are cut by a transversal. The transversal creates segments of 8 between the first and second parallel lines, and 12 between the second and third parallel lines. A second transversal cuts the same three parallel lines, creating a segment of 10 between the first and second parallel lines. What is the length of the segment between the second and third parallel lines on the second transversal?
questions.explanation: By the Intercept Theorem, corresponding segments on two transversals cut by parallel lines are proportional: 8/12 = 10/x → x = (12 × 10)/8 = 120/8 = 15.
questions.trap: Students assume the second transversal also has a 12-unit segment (since 12 appears in the first transversal) or add/subtract rather than using proportionality.
questions.ets_note: Plain textbook intercept-theorem setup; no figure.

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. Two angles lie between the parallel lines and on the same side of the transversal, one at each line, and measure (3x + 10)° and (x + 50)°. What is x?
questions.explanation: Co-interior angles are supplementary: (3x + 10) + (x + 50) = 180 → 4x + 60 = 180 → 4x = 120 → x = 30.
questions.trap: Students set the angles equal (3x + 10 = x + 50 → 2x = 40 → x = 20), treating co-interior angles as alternate interior angles.
questions.ets_note: No figure; which angle is paired is unclear. 'Co-interior' is not ETS terminology.

changes: replaced undefined 'angle between transversal and first line'/'co-interior' with explicit position: between the lines, same side of transversal

questions.question:
In triangle PQR, line ST is parallel to QR with S on PQ and T on PR. PS = 4, SQ = 6.
Quantity A: The ratio ST/QR
Quantity B: 2/5
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: By the Triangle Proportionality Theorem, ST/QR = PS/PQ. PQ = PS + SQ = 4 + 6 = 10. So ST/QR = 4/10 = 2/5. Quantity A = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students compute PS/SQ = 4/6 = 2/3 as the ratio, using the part-to-part ratio instead of the part-to-whole ratio PS/PQ.

questions.question: Lines r and s are parallel. Transversal t makes an angle of α with line r, and transversal u makes an angle of β with line r, each measured above the line and to the right of the transversal. Which of the following correctly describes the angles that t and u make with line s, measured in the same position (above s and to the right of the transversal)?
options: A. Both angles equal 180° − α and 180° − β respectively
B. The angles equal α and β respectively
C. The angles equal β and α (swapped)
E. The angles equal α and β only if t and u are parallel to each other
questions.explanation: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal. Transversal t makes angle α with r, so in the corresponding position it makes angle α with s. Independently, transversal u makes angle β with r and therefore β with s. Each transversal is treated on its own; the presence of a second transversal changes nothing.
questions.trap: Choice A applies the co-interior (same-side interior) rule and subtracts from 180°, although the angles described are in corresponding, not co-interior, positions. Choice C assumes two transversals exchange their angles. Choice D averages the two angles, as if the transversals interacted. Choice E adds a condition that is never needed: corresponding angles are equal because r and s are parallel, whatever the relationship between t and u.
questions.ets_note: 'Angle with line' undefined; A and B both defensible depending on side; abstract textbook phrasing.

changes: fixed the side/position in which each angle is measured so A vs B is not ambiguous
replaced banned 'E. The angles cannot be determined without more information' with a false conditional that encodes the belief that both transversals must be parallel
rewrote explanation and trap to cover every distractor
answer unchanged: B

questions.question: Lines a and b are parallel, cut by transversal t. Angle 1 is an acute angle at line a that lies between the two lines. Select ALL statements that are true.
options: A. The corresponding angle at line b equals Angle 1
B. The co-interior angle at line b equals Angle 1
C. The alternate interior angle at line b equals Angle 1
D. The co-interior angle at line b equals 180° − Angle 1
E. The angle at line b vertically opposite the alternate interior angle equals Angle 1
questions.explanation: A: Corresponding angles are equal — TRUE. B: Co-interior angles are supplementary, not equal — FALSE (Angle 1 is acute so 180° − Angle 1 ≠ Angle 1). C: Alternate interior angles are equal — TRUE. D: Co-interior angles sum to 180°, so the co-interior angle = 180° − Angle 1 — TRUE. E: The alternate interior angle equals Angle 1, and its vertically opposite angle equals it — TRUE.
questions.trap: Students include B, thinking co-interior angles are equal like alternate interior. Co-interior is the one named-pair relationship that is supplementary, not equal.
questions.ets_note: Without a figure the stem is ambiguous; C and E are mutually exclusive readings, but the key marks both true.

changes: stated Angle 1 lies between the lines so interior-angle relationships are defined
reworded E, which used an exterior-angle relationship undefined for an interior Angle 1, to an equivalent true statement
explanation updated

ets_key_resolved.verdict: key confirmed by independent re-solve of the current stem
ets_key_resolved.note: dispute flag was left over from the original audit; the stem had since been rewritten or the original objection did not hold

questions.question: In triangle XYZ, a line parallel to YZ intersects XY at point A and XZ at point B. If XA = 5, XY = 20, and YZ = 24, what is the length of AB?
questions.explanation: By the Triangle Proportionality Theorem, AB/YZ = XA/XY = 5/20 = 1/4. So AB = (1/4) × 24 = 6.
questions.trap: Students use XA/AY = AB/YZ: AY = 20 − 5 = 15, so 5/15 = 1/3, giving AB = 8. This uses the part-to-remaining ratio instead of the part-to-whole ratio.

questions.question: Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One pair of co-interior angles are (3y + 18)° and (2y + 12)°. What is the value of y?
questions.trap: Students set the expressions equal (3y + 18 = 2y + 12 → y = −6), treating them as alternate interior angles instead of co-interior.

questions.question:
Lines c and d are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Angle P, at line c, measures 65°. Angle Q, at line d, lies between the two lines and on the same side of t as angle P.
Quantity A: The measure of angle Q
Quantity B: 115°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Angles P and Q lie between the parallel lines on the same side of the transversal, so they are supplementary. Q = 180° − 65° = 115°, which equals Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students may assume Q = P (confusing these with alternate interior angles), giving Q = 65° and choosing B.
questions.ets_note: Quantity B restates the co-interior definition; tautological. No figure; easy not medium.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Co-interior angles sum to 180; the quantities are the same expression.

changes: Quantity B was a restatement of the angle relationship; replaced with 115° so the solver must find the angle relationship

questions.question: A transversal cuts parallel lines l and m. At line l, the angle below the line and to the right of the transversal is 48°. Which of the following must equal 132°?
options: A. The alternate interior angle at m
B. The corresponding angle at m
C. The co-interior angle at m on the right side
D. The vertical angle at l
E. The angle at m that is alternate exterior to the vertical angle at l
questions.explanation: The given angle lies between the parallel lines and measures 48°. Co-interior angles on the same side (right side) sum to 180°: co-interior = 180° − 48° = 132°. The alternate interior angle (A), the corresponding angle (B), the vertical angle (D), and the angle alternate exterior to that vertical angle (E) each equal 48°. Only C gives 132°.
questions.trap: Students choose A or B, not recognizing that alternate interior and corresponding angles are equal to the original (48°), not supplementary.
questions.ets_note: Given angle lies outside the strip, so 'alternate interior/co-interior at m' is loosely defined; strictly the right-side interior angle at m is 48.

changes: moved the given 48° angle from above l to below l so it is an interior angle and 'alternate/co-interior at m' are well defined
reworded E so it names a unique angle (value 48°)
explanation updated

questions.question: Three parallel lines l₁, l₂, and l₃ are cut by two transversals. The first transversal creates segments of 6 (between l₁–l₂) and 9 (between l₂–l₃). The second transversal creates a segment of 8 between l₁ and l₂. What is the length of the segment of the second transversal between l₂ and l₃?
questions.explanation: By the intercept theorem, the ratios of corresponding segments on two transversals are equal: 6/9 = 8/x → x = (8 × 9)/6 = 72/6 = 12.
questions.trap: Students compute 6/8 = 9/x → x = 12 (coincidentally correct with a wrong setup). The standard error is additive: 8 + (9 − 6) = 11, or simply stating x = 9 by analogy.
questions.ets_note: Trap calls the 6/8=9/x setup wrong yet it is the correct setup; no figure.

questions.question: Lines p and q are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Angle x is an interior angle formed at line p. Select ALL angles that are always equal to x.
options: A. Vertically opposite angle to x at line p
B. Corresponding angle at line q
C. Alternate interior angle at line q
D. Co-interior angle at line q
E. Angle at line q vertically opposite the alternate interior angle
questions.explanation: A: Vertical angles are equal. B: Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel. C: Alternate interior angles are equal. D: Co-interior angles are supplementary, not equal. E: The angle vertically opposite the alternate interior angle is equal to it, hence equal to x.
questions.trap: Students include D, believing all named angle pairs with parallel lines are equal. Co-interior is the exception — supplementary, not equal.
questions.ets_note: No figure or labelled angles; 'Angle x at line p' is undefined, making alternate interior/exterior ambiguous.

changes: stated x is an interior angle so 'alternate interior' is defined
replaced option E ('alternate exterior' is undefined for an interior x) with an equivalent well-defined true statement

questions.question:
In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC, with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 3, DB = 5. The area of triangle ABC = 100.
Quantity A: Area of trapezoid BCED
Quantity B: 9/64 × Area of triangle ABC
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: AD/AB = 3/(3+5) = 3/8. Area ratio (ADE):(ABC) = (3/8)² = 9/64. Area of ADE = 9/64 × 100 = 14.0625. Area of trapezoid BCED = 100 − 14.0625 = 85.9375. Quantity B = 9/64 × 100 = 14.0625. Quantity A (85.9375) > Quantity B (14.0625).
questions.trap: Students compute area ratio as AD/DB = 3/5 (part-to-part) instead of AD/AB = 3/8 (part-to-whole), getting (3/5)² = 9/25 for the area ratio of ADE, and then confusingly compare it to Quantity B.
questions.ets_note: Quantity B is just the small triangle's area, oddly framed; trap text does not match a real comparison.

questions.question: Lines a and b are parallel. A transversal t crosses both, making an angle of 70° with a. A second line s (not parallel to t) also crosses both, making an angle of 50° with a (on the same side as t). What is the acute angle between t and s, measured at their intersection between the parallel lines?
questions.explanation: Both transversals cross line a making angles of 70° and 50° with it. The angle between the two transversals at their intersection = |70° − 50°| = 20°. This follows from the exterior angle relationship in the triangle formed by a, t, and s: the angle at the intersection of t and s equals the difference of the angles they make with the parallel line a.
questions.trap: Students add the angles (70° + 50° = 120°) and take the supplement (60°) or complement, not recognizing that the angle between two transversals equals the absolute difference of their angles with the parallel lines.
questions.ets_note: Configuration of t and s unspecified; answer 20 relies on interpretation; no figure.

questions.question: Line m is parallel to line n. A transversal cuts m at point A, creating interior angle ∠1 = (4x)°. At point B on line n, ∠2 is the alternate interior angle to ∠1. A third line through A makes angle ∠3 = (2x + 12)° with line m, adjacent to ∠1. If ∠1 + ∠3 = 180°, what is the measure of ∠2?
questions.explanation: ∠1 + ∠3 = 180°: 4x + 2x + 12 = 180 → 6x = 168 → x = 28. ∠1 = 4(28) = 112°. Since ∠2 is the alternate interior angle to ∠1, and alternate interior angles are equal: ∠2 = 112°.
questions.trap: Students compute ∠2 = 180° − ∠1 = 68°, thinking alternate interior angles are supplementary instead of equal.
questions.ets_note: Convoluted no-figure setup; 'find' wording; stem hands over the equation; ∠3 adds nothing.

changes: stated that ∠1 is an interior angle so an alternate interior angle exists
ETS phrasing for final question

questions.question:
Lines f and g are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Let x be the measure of an angle formed by t and f, where x is not given. Let y be the measure of the angle at g that is a same-side interior angle with x, and let z be the measure of the angle at g that is an alternate interior angle with x.

Quantity A: x + y
Quantity B: 2z
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Quantity A: x and y are same-side interior angles, so x + y = 180°. Quantity B: alternate interior angles are equal, so z = x and 2z = 2x. If x = 90°, both quantities equal 180°. If x = 70°, Quantity A = 180° and Quantity B = 140°. Since x is not fixed, the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Students use the same-side interior angle for z, getting Quantity B = 2(180° − x) = 360° − 2x, and then wrongly conclude the quantities are equal or that one is always greater.
questions.ets_note: Never says B is co-interior to A; no figure; contrived angle labels.

changes: renamed angles x,y,z to stop clashing with Quantity A/B labels
stated y is same-side interior to x and z alternate interior to x
rewrote explanation and trap in new variables

questions.question: In triangle ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC such that DE ∥ BC. If the area of triangle ADE is 36 and the area of trapezoid BCED is 64, what is the length of DE if BC = 20?
questions.explanation: Area of triangle ABC = 36 + 64 = 100. Since DE ∥ BC, triangles ADE and ABC are similar. Ratio of areas = (DE/BC)² = 36/100 = 9/25. So DE/BC = 3/5. DE = (3/5) × 20 = 12.
questions.trap: Students compute the ratio of areas as 36/64 (ADE to trapezoid) instead of 36/100 (ADE to whole triangle ABC), getting DE/BC = 6/8 = 3/4, so DE = 15 — option D.
questions.ets_note: One similarity step; 'hard' overstated. Clean numbers otherwise.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Add areas to get 100, square-root ratio gives 3/5, scale BC; similar to anchor 030.

questions.question: Lines l₁, l₂, l₃, and l₄ are all parallel. Two transversals cut these four lines. On the first transversal, the segments between consecutive parallel lines are 3, 5, and 7 (from l₁ to l₄). On the second transversal, the first segment (between l₁ and l₂) has length 6. What is the total length of the second transversal between l₁ and l₄?
questions.explanation: By the intercept theorem, corresponding segments on two transversals cut by parallel lines are proportional. The scale factor = 6/3 = 2. So second transversal: l₂–l₃ = 2×5 = 10, l₃–l₄ = 2×7 = 14. Total = 6 + 10 + 14 = 30.
questions.trap: Students find the scale factor correctly (2) but apply it to the total of the first transversal (15 × 2 = 30) without checking — coincidentally correct here. The real trap is students who use only the ratio 3/5 = 6/x to find the second segment (x = 10), then stop without adding all three segments.
questions.ets_note: Single proportion labelled hard; trap text is muddled.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Proportional segments on two transversals: scale factor 2, then sum; same as anchor 019.

questions.question:
Lines j and k are parallel. Two transversals t₁ and t₂ intersect each other at point P between j and k, and form a triangle with line j. The interior angles of this triangle at line j are 40° (at t₁) and 30° (at t₂).

Quantity A: The acute angle between t₁ and t₂ at P
Quantity B: 10°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: In the triangle formed by line j and the two transversals t₁ and t₂: interior angles at j are 40° and 30°. The angle at P = 180° − 40° − 30° = 110° (the interior angle of the triangle at P). The acute angle between t₁ and t₂ = 180° − 110° = 70°. Quantity A = 70° > Quantity B = 10°.
questions.trap: Students subtract the two angles: 40° − 30° = 10° as the angle between the transversals, choosing C. The correct approach uses the triangle angle sum: the angle at P = 180° − 40° − 30° = 110°, and the acute supplement is 70°.
questions.ets_note: Orientation of transversals unspecified; angle at P is 10 or 70, key assumes one reading.

changes: replaced 'same side' orientation phrase with an explicit triangle description, fixing the angle at 70° (not 10°)

ets_key_resolved.verdict: key confirmed by independent re-solve of the current stem
ets_key_resolved.note: dispute flag was left over from the original audit; the stem had since been rewritten or the original objection did not hold

questions.question: AB ∥ CD. Point E lies between the two parallel lines. Angle ABE = 35° and angle CDE = 50°. What is the measure of angle BED?
questions.explanation: Draw a line EF through E parallel to AB (and CD). Since EF ∥ AB, angle ABE and angle BEF are alternate interior angles → angle BEF = 35°. Since EF ∥ CD, angle CDE and angle DEF are alternate interior angles → angle DEF = 50°. Angle BED = angle BEF + angle DEF = 35° + 50° = 85°.
questions.trap: Students incorrectly use co-interior angles: 180° − 35° = 145° or 180° − 50° = 130°, then try to combine them and arrive at 95° (choosing D). The key insight is to draw an auxiliary line through E parallel to both AB and CD.
questions.ets_note: Configuration depends on an unseen figure; other placements give 165 or other values.

questions.question: Lines m and n are parallel, cut by transversal t. At the intersection with m, four angles are labeled 1 (top-left), 2 (top-right), 3 (bottom-right), 4 (bottom-left) going clockwise. At the intersection with n, four angles are labeled 5 (top-left), 6 (top-right), 7 (bottom-right), 8 (bottom-left). Angle 1 = 70°. Select ALL correct statements.
questions.explanation: With angle 1 = 70° (top-left at m): Vertical angles: angle 3 = 70° (bottom-right at m). Supplementary: angle 2 = angle 4 = 110°. At line n (corresponding): angle 5 = 70° (top-left, corresponding to 1). Angle 7 = 70° (vertical to 5). Angle 6 = 110° (top-right at n). Angle 8 = 110° (bottom-left at n). A ✓, B ✓, C ✓, D: angle 3 = 70° (not 110°) ✗, E ✓.
questions.trap: Students confuse which angles are vertical vs supplementary at the second intersection, especially labeling angle 3 as 110° (it is 70°, being vertical to angle 1).
questions.ets_note: Basic angle chasing labelled hard; no figure, positions only described.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Apply vertical, supplementary and corresponding relations to check five statements.

questions.question: Lines a, b, and c are all parallel. Two transversals cut these three lines. On the first transversal, the segment between a and b is 4 and the segment between b and c is 6. On the second transversal, the total segment between a and c is 25. What is the length of the segment of the second transversal between a and b?
questions.explanation: By the intercept theorem, the ratio a–b : b–c = 4:6 = 2:3 for both transversals. The total a–c on the second transversal = 25. Part between a and b = (2/5) × 25 = 10.
questions.trap: Students compute 4/6 = x/(25−x), solving correctly to get x = 10. The common error is setting 4/6 = x/25 (using total instead of remaining part) → x = 100/6 ≈ 16.7.
questions.ets_note: Two-transversal setup is described in words with no figure; single proportion labelled hard.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Intercept theorem ratio 2:3, then a share of 25.

questions.question: Lines AB and CD are parallel. Transversal t crosses AB at P making angle APT = (4x + 5)° above AB (where T is a point on t above AB). It crosses CD at Q making the corresponding angle CQT = (6x − 15)° above CD. What is the measure of angle APT?
questions.explanation: Corresponding angles are equal: 4x + 5 = 6x − 15 → 20 = 2x → x = 10. Angle APT = 4(10) + 5 = 45°. Verify: 6(10) − 15 = 45°. ✓
questions.trap: Students add the expressions to 180° (treating them as co-interior angles): 4x + 5 + 6x − 15 = 180 → 10x − 10 = 180 → x = 19, giving angle APT = 81° — not matching any option cleanly.
questions.ets_note: One linear equation labelled hard; no figure.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Set corresponding angles equal, solve linear equation, substitute.

questions.question:
In triangle ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC such that DE ∥ BC. The ratio AD:AB = 2:5. The area of triangle ABC = 100.
Quantity A: Area of trapezoid BCED
Quantity B: 60
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: AD/AB = 2/5. Area ratio (ADE):(ABC) = (AD/AB)² = (2/5)² = 4/25. Area of ADE = 4/25 × 100 = 16. Area of trapezoid BCED = 100 − 16 = 84. Quantity A = 84 > Quantity B = 60.
questions.trap: Students compute area ratio as AD/AB = 2/5 (using the linear ratio instead of squaring it), getting area ADE = 40, trapezoid = 60, and selecting C.

questions.question: Two parallel lines l and m are cut by two transversals t₁ and t₂. The transversals intersect each other at point P, which lies between the two parallel lines. On line l: t₁ intersects at A, t₂ intersects at B. On line m: t₁ intersects at C, t₂ intersects at D. Given AP = 6, PC = 9, and BP = 4, what is PD?
questions.explanation: Triangles APB and CPD are similar (vertical angles at P are equal; since l ∥ m, alternate interior angles give ∠PAB = ∠PCD and ∠PBA = ∠PDC). By similar triangles: AP/CP = BP/DP → 6/9 = 4/DP → DP = (9 × 4)/6 = 6.
questions.trap: Students try to use the intercept theorem directly along the parallel lines instead of the similar triangles at the intersection, or incorrectly set up AP × DP = BP × CP (power of a point, valid for circles but not here), getting DP = 13.5.
questions.ets_note: No figure for transversal setup; trap's power-of-point formula inconsistent with its 13.5.

questions.question: Three parallel horizontal lines m, n, and p are cut by two transversals, both of which slope upward from left to right. Transversal t₁ makes a 60° angle with each parallel line. Transversal t₂ makes a 45° angle with each parallel line. These two transversals intersect between lines m and n at point Q. What is the acute angle formed at Q between the two transversals?
questions.explanation: Each transversal makes a fixed angle with the parallel lines — 60° and 45°. At their point of intersection, the angle between the two transversals is the difference: 60° − 45° = 15°.
questions.trap: Students add: 60° + 45° = 105°, then take supplement or half. The correct result is the difference of the angles the transversals make with the parallel lines.
questions.ets_note: Transversal orientation unspecified; acute angle could be 15 or 75. Key assumes same direction.

changes: added that both transversals slope upward left to right (opposite slopes give 75°)

questions.question: Lines a ∥ b. Transversal t creates angles with a and b. A second transversal s (not parallel to t) also cuts a and b at different points. Select ALL statements that are always true.
options: A. Corresponding angles formed by t with a and b are equal
B. The angle that t makes with a equals the angle s makes with b
C. Co-interior angles formed by s with a and b sum to 180°
D. Alternate interior angles formed by t are equal to alternate interior angles formed by s
E. Alternate exterior angles formed by t with a and b are equal to each other
questions.explanation: A: Corresponding angles are always equal for any transversal crossing parallel lines — TRUE. B: The angle t makes with a need not equal the angle s makes with b (s is an independent transversal) — FALSE. C: Co-interior angles for any transversal crossing parallel lines sum to 180° — TRUE for s as well. D: Alternate interior angles for t are equal to each other, and those for s are equal to each other, but the angles for t and s need not be equal — FALSE. E: Alternate exterior angles formed by a single transversal with parallel lines are always equal — TRUE.
questions.trap: Students include B or D, thinking all transversal angles with the same pair of parallel lines are related to each other. Each transversal is independent — its angles depend on its slope.
questions.ets_note: Mostly textbook parallel-line facts, no figure; hard label overstated.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Judge five statements about angles from two transversals; conceptual but each is routine.

questions.question:
PQ ∥ RS. Point T is above line PQ. Lines TP and TQ meet PQ at P and Q, making angle TPQ = 50° and angle TQP = 70°. A perpendicular from T to line RS meets RS at point F.

Quantity A: Angle PTQ
Quantity B: 60°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: In triangle TPQ: angle TPQ = 50°, angle TQP = 70°. Angle PTQ = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°. The perpendicular from T to RS is a red herring — PQ ∥ RS, so the perpendicular distance is fixed, but it doesn't affect angle PTQ. Quantity A = 60° = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students are distracted by the mention of PQ ∥ RS and the perpendicular to RS, and attempt to apply parallel-line angle rules instead of simply using the angle sum in triangle TPQ.
questions.ets_note: Perpendicular and PQ parallel RS are pure red herrings with no figure; slightly contrived.

questions.question: Lines l1 || l2 || l3. Transversal t1 intersects them at A (on l1), B (on l2), C (on l3) with AB = 6 and BC = 9. Transversal t2 intersects them at D (on l1), E (on l2), F (on l3) with DE = 6. The distance AD along l1 is 6. A line drawn from A through E is extended to meet l3 at point G. What is the length FG?
questions.explanation: Step 1: By the intercept theorem, AB/BC = DE/EF → 6/9 = 6/EF → EF = 9. Step 2: Set up coordinates. Let l₁:y=15, l₂:y=9, l₃:y=0 (vertical separations matching AB=6, BC=9). With both transversals vertical: A=(0,15), B=(0,9), C=(0,0) on t₁; D=(6,15), E=(6,9), F=(6,0) on t₂ (DE=6 ✓, EF=9 ✓). Step 3: Line AEG passes through A=(0,15) and E=(6,9). Slope = (9−15)/(6−0) = −1. Equation: y = 15 − x. At l₃ (y=0): x = 15. So G = (15, 0). Step 4: FG = |15 − 6| = 9.
questions.trap: Students find EF = 9 and immediately choose 9 as 'the answer for GF' without completing the coordinate geometry step to find where line AE extended meets l₃. They confuse FG with EF.
questions.ets_note: Missing data: answer needs AD (or perpendicular transversals) which is unstated; key silently assumes vertical transversals.

questions.question: Lines a || b || c. Transversal t cuts them at A (on a), B (on b), C (on c) with AB:BC = 2:3. A second transversal s cuts them at D (on a), E (on b), F (on c). The two transversals t and s intersect at B = E (i.e., they meet at the same point on b). DB = 6, BF = 9, and DA = 6. A point G is on segment DA such that DG:GA = 1:2. The line through G and B extended meets c at H. What is CH?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Since both transversals meet at B on line b, we can set up coordinates with B at the origin. Let a be above b at height 2k and c be below b at height 3k (ratio AB:BC = 2:3). Step 2: t (first transversal) is vertical: A=(0,2k), B=(0,0), C=(0,−3k). s (second transversal): DB=6 so D is at distance 6 from B on line a: the line BD makes some angle θ with a. D=(−6cosα, 2k) on a (where α is the angle BD makes with the vertical). Similarly, BF=9 so F=(9cosα, −3k)/... This gets complicated without fixing the angle. I will instead write a purely self-contained, determinate extreme-hard problem.
questions.trap: Students apply the intercept theorem using only the ratio AB:BC without tracking which point G maps to on line c.
questions.ets_note: No figure; required length not determined; key explanation admits the problem is broken.
questions.ets_withdraw_reason: Underdetermined: CH equals the horizontal offset between A and D, which is not given; DB = 6 and BF = 9 do not fix it. The stored explanation admits it is broken.

questions.question:
Lines a ∥ b. Two transversals t₁ and t₂ intersect each other at point P between the parallel lines. t₁ meets a at A and b at B. t₂ meets a at C and b at D. AP = 3, PB = 5, CP = 4.
Quantity A: PD
Quantity B: 20/3
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Triangles APC and BPD are similar (∠APC = ∠BPD as vertical angles; ∠PAC = ∠PBD as alternate interior angles since a ∥ b). By similarity: AP/BP = CP/PD → 3/5 = 4/PD → PD = (5 × 4)/3 = 20/3. Quantity A = 20/3 = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students use AP × PD = BP × CP (power of a point, which applies to circles, not parallel lines), getting 3 × PD = 5 × 4 → PD = 20/3 (coincidentally correct but wrong reasoning). The real error trap: students set AP/CP = BP/PD → 3/4 = 5/PD → PD = 20/3 (also correct! This is the same ratio). The dangerous trap: students set AP + PB = CP + PD → 8 = 4 + PD → PD = 4, choosing B.
questions.ets_note: Medium item labelled extreme_hard; trap text rambles and self-contradicts.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Vertical and alternate angles give similar triangles, then one proportion.

questions.question: PQ ∥ RS. T is a point above PQ. Lines from T through P and Q are extended to meet RS at U and V respectively (making TPU and TQV straight lines). Given TP = 6, PU = 9, TQ = 8, and QV = 12, what is the ratio PQ:UV?
questions.explanation: Because PQ ∥ UV and T is the common vertex, triangle TPQ is similar to triangle TUV. The similarity ratio is TP/TU = 6/(6 + 9) = 6/15 = 2/5, confirmed by TQ/TV = 8/(8 + 12) = 8/20 = 2/5. Corresponding sides scale by the same factor, so PQ:UV = 2:5.
questions.trap: Choice D, 2:3, uses the segment ratio TP:PU = 6:9 instead of TP:TU. Choice C, 3:5, uses PU:TU = 9:15, the wrong part of the divided side. Choice B, 1:2, pairs mismatched sides, TP:QV = 6:12. Choice E inverts the ratio and reports UV:PQ.
questions.ets_note: MCQ has 'Cannot be determined' option; ratios unordered; no figure; extreme_hard overstated.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Identify similar triangles TPQ and TUV, compute 6/15; one similarity with a consistency check.

changes: replaced banned 'E. Cannot be determined' with 5:2, the inverted ratio
re-sorted the ratio options into ascending numeric value: 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.667, 2.5
answer moves from B to A by ordering; the correct value 2:5 is unchanged

questions.question: Lines j and k are parallel. Transversals t₁ and t₂ intersect each other at a point M between j and k. t₁ meets j at A and k at B, and t₂ meets j at C and k at D. If AM = 4, MB = 6 and CM = 3, what is the length of MD?
questions.explanation: Angle AMC = angle BMD (vertical angles) and angle MAC = angle MBD (alternate interior angles for parallel lines j and k cut by t₁). So triangle AMC is similar to triangle BMD with A↔B and C↔D, giving AM/BM = CM/DM. Then 4/6 = 3/MD, so MD = 18/4 = 4.5.
questions.trap: Using the whole segment AB = 10 in place of MB (4/10 = 3/MD gives 7.5, choice E), or copying a length straight across, taking MD = AM = 4 or MD = MB = 6, as if the transversals were cut into equal lengths rather than in equal ratio.
questions.ets_note: Premise inconsistent: MD is forced by j parallel k, and the AC parallel BD condition is vacuous; single correct option, degenerate select-all.

changes: removed the vacuous condition: the stem asked for the values of MD making AC ∥ BD, but AC lies on j and BD on k, which are parallel by hypothesis, so the condition held for every MD and the stored explanation had to appeal to an unstated consistency requirement instead
the stem now asks which values MD could have, which is the question the similar-triangles proportion actually answers, and the answer is still 4.5 only
rewrote the explanation to derive the similarity from the vertical angles at M and the alternate interior angles, rather than asserting it

NOT fixable without moving the key: exactly one option is correct, which rule 1.2 counts as a degenerate select-all. The item should be converted to a five-option MCQ or to numeric entry, which is a type change for the key-owning pass.
converted to single-answer MCQ; similar triangles fix MD uniquely
stem 'Indicate all such values' replaced with 'what is'
